### Question 1

A fall is defined by where the person ends up, not by how badly it turned out. If someone reaches the floor when they did not mean to, it counts, even if a nurse had hold of them the whole way down and even if nothing hurts afterward. That may seem like over-counting, but it is the point: the harmless landings and the broken hips come from the same underlying problem, and the harmless ones are far more common, so they are the early signal. If you only counted injuries, you would be waiting for someone to get hurt before you could see the pattern.

### Question 2

Universal precautions answer a simple question: what should be true in every room, for every patient, before anyone even looks at a risk score? Bed low, brakes on, call light within arm's reach, path to the bathroom clear and lit, shoes that grip. These are cheap, they inconvenience no one, and they help the patient whose score was low but whose blood pressure drops on the third day of a new medication. Screening is imperfect, so the baseline exists to catch the people screening misses. Patients who do screen high then get extra, specific help layered on top.

### Question 3

Sort every risk by whether it travels with the person or stays behind in the room. Weak legs, wobbly blood pressure, and cloudy vision go wherever the patient goes, so they are intrinsic. A dark hallway with cords across it stays put, so it is extrinsic. The sorting matters because it tells you who fixes the problem and how fast: an environmental hazard can be gone in two minutes with a light switch and a cord cover, while weak legs take weeks of therapy. And notice that neither one alone usually causes the fall. Strong legs handle a dark hallway; weak legs in a clear, lit room usually manage too. It is the combination that puts people down.

### Question 4

When your foot catches on something, you do not decide to catch yourself; a reflex fires and your other leg swings out before you have consciously registered the trip. That reflex is fast, and its speed is the whole margin of safety. Sedating medications turn down the speed of the nervous system, so the same reflex still happens but arrives a beat late, and a beat late is a landing instead of a save. The medication does not push anyone over. It removes the automatic rescue that normally follows the push, which is why the fix is often lowering the dose or switching drugs rather than adding equipment.

### Question 5

Standing up is a small circulatory emergency that your body normally solves before you notice it. The instant you rise, roughly half a liter of blood drifts downward into your legs, and the pressure available to your brain dips. Healthy vessels clamp down and the heart speeds up within a couple of heartbeats, so nothing happens. If illness, bed rest, or blood pressure medication weakens that response, the dip lasts several seconds instead, and those seconds happen while the person is standing at the bedside with nothing to hold. Taking the pressure lying and then standing is how you find the dip in advance, before it is discovered on the floor.

### Question 6

The same piece of metal can be a handle or a fence, and which one it is depends entirely on why it was raised. One rail up gives a patient something to pull against while rolling over, which supports movement. All four up to stop someone from leaving is a barrier, and confused patients who want out do not reason with barriers, they climb. Now the drop starts from the top of the rail rather than the edge of a low mattress, and there are gaps between rail, mattress, and frame where a limb or neck can wedge. That is why the regulation looks at intent: a device meant to keep someone in is a restraint whether or not they complained about it.

### Question 7

Avoiding walking looks protective and is actually the trap. Sit more and the legs get weaker, so standing feels shakier, so sitting looks even more sensible, and the spiral tightens. The critical detail is that nobody can restrict activity to zero. Everyone still gets up for the bathroom, and when that trip finally happens it happens on the weakest legs the person has ever had, often at night, in a hurry. So the fear does not remove the risky moments, it just concentrates them and removes the strength that would have handled them. The exit is counterintuitive: supervised practice at moving, not more rest.

### Question 8

The TUG is a compressed obstacle course: rise from a chair, walk about ten feet, turn, walk back, sit. It packs strength, balance, turning, and reaction into one number, and CDC's cutoff is twelve seconds. Fifteen means the screen is positive, and that is all it means. A positive screen is a pointer, not an explanation, because the same slow time could come from arthritic knees, a sedating medication, poor vision, or fear of falling, and each of those needs a different fix. So the correct response is to keep looking, then treat what you find, usually with exercise and strengthening rather than with rest.

### Question 9

Two separate jobs hide inside the phrase fall safety: stop the crash, and soften the crash. Clearing the path, reviewing sedating medications, and keeping the call light in reach all try to stop it. A padded mat next to a bed lowered to its floor position does nothing at all unless a fall is already happening, which is exactly what makes it injury prevention rather than fall prevention. It is the helmet, not the riding lesson. You want both, because in a hospital full of weak, medicated, unfamiliar-with-the-room patients, some falls will get through, and whether one of them breaks a hip depends on how far the body drops and what it lands on.

### Question 10

A full bladder is not a negotiable request. Tell a patient a hundred times to call for help and they will still get up alone, at 3 a.m., in socks, towing an IV pole, because waiting is not something the body offers as an option. So the strategy is not to make people wait better, it is to arrive before the urgency builds. Checking in on a fixed rhythm and asking about the bathroom, pain, and position means the need is handled while it is still small. Rounding does also mean someone finds a fallen patient sooner, which is worth something, but that is damage control; the falls avoided are the ones that never started.

### Question 11

A forecast of a ninety percent chance of rain keeps nobody dry. Someone still has to pick up the umbrella. A fall-risk score is that forecast, and the common failure mode in real units is that the number gets charted, the box gets checked for the audit, and nothing downstream changes, because the score does not name what to do. High risk from urgent toileting needs and high risk from a sedating sleep medication produce the same number but require completely different actions, one a two-hour bathroom schedule and the other a call to the prescriber. Swapping to a fancier scale would not help either, since no tool has proven clearly better than the rest at predicting who falls.

### Question 12

Both of these feel like solutions and neither carries its weight. Restraints trade one hazard for several: muscle wastes fast in someone who cannot move, skin breaks down, confusion worsens, and a patient fighting the straps can injure themselves worse than any fall would have. Alarms fail for a different reason. Watch what an alarm actually does in time order: the patient sits up, swings their legs over, the sensor triggers, and now the beep and the fall are racing each other down a hallway. If no one is within a few seconds' reach, the alarm simply announces what already happened. What works is unglamorous: check in before the need becomes urgent, keep the legs strong, lower the bed, pad the floor.
